messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Navy Officer
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Rodrigo is a 55-year-old Cuban American Navy officer currently stationed at a shore command on the East Coast, where he has served for nearly three decades. He presents for intake following a referral from his unit's medical officer, though he acknowledges that he delayed seeking help for close to two years after the event that brought him here. He lives with his long-term partner, describes the relationship as stable but strained, and carries himself with the composed bearing of a man accustomed to managing what he feels in front of others.

Approximately twenty-six months ago, Rodrigo was attached to a multinational coordination team operating in a conflict-affected region in Central America, serving in a liaison capacity that was officially classified as non-combat. The team was accompanying a convoy of civilian aid workers through a corridor that had been assessed as relatively secure. Rodrigo was in the lead vehicle when the convoy was stopped at an improvised checkpoint manned by an armed faction. What followed unfolded over approximately forty minutes. He watched from a position of enforced stillness — unarmed, under explicit orders not to escalate, surrounded by men with weapons — as several of the aid workers were separated from the group, beaten, and led away. He could hear a woman calling out in Spanish. He did not move. The convoy was eventually released, but three of the aid workers were never recovered.

In the weeks that followed, Rodrigo noticed that the memory of those forty minutes did not behave like other difficult memories he had accumulated over a long career. It did not recede. At unpredictable moments — most often when he was driving on base, monitoring a radio channel, or sitting in a briefing room listening to a voice with a particular timbre — the scene returned with a completeness that stunned him. He has described these episodes as feeling entirely real across every sense simultaneously: the smell of red dust and diesel, the specific quality of afternoon light, the sound of that woman's voice. In those moments, he is not remembering so much as he is back there, motionless, watching. At other times, when he attempts to think through the event deliberately — as he has done many times, trying to make sense of it — he finds himself recalling the sequence with strange detachment, as though reviewing an incident report about someone else entirely. This alternation between overwhelming immersion and hollow numbness has left him deeply unsettled about his own mind.

What Rodrigo finds most unbearable, however, is not the intrusions themselves but what he has come to believe about what they mean. He is certain that a stronger man — a better officer — would have found a way to act. He has returned to those forty minutes hundreds of times in his mind, cataloguing the moments at which he might have intervened, and each review deepens his conviction that his stillness was not tactical compliance but personal failure. He will never forgive himself, he says plainly, for not doing more to stop what happened. The belief that he should have protected those people and did not sits in him like something structural, not like a thought he could revise. Alongside this is a quieter, more corrosive certainty: that the paralysis he showed that day reflects something essentially weak in him, a flaw that his career and his uniform had simply concealed until that afternoon made it visible.

These beliefs have shaped his days in ways that have compounded over time. He has withdrawn from the junior officers he once mentored, finding it intolerable to occupy a position of authority that he no longer feels he has earned. His partner has noticed his remoteness and has named it directly; Rodrigo has not been able to explain what is happening, partly because he fears that articulating it will confirm it. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment last month during a routine training exercise when a junior officer asked him directly what he would do if ordered not to intervene in a dangerous situation. Rodrigo found he could not answer. He stood there in silence long enough that the room noticed. He is most afraid, he says, that therapy will prove to him what he already suspects — that there is no version of events in which he was not, simply, a coward.
